xep.header:
Multiparty Jingle (Muji) — monocles profile
This specification defines an XMPP protocol extension for initiating and managing multiparty voice and video conferences within an XMPP MUC. This revision is the monocles chat profile of XEP-0272: it keeps the wire format of version 0.2.0 and adds the participant-authentication, DTLS-fingerprint protection (OMEMO / post-quantum OMEMO2), mesh-maintenance, presence-persistence, privacy and resource-limit rules implemented by monocles chat (Android and desktop).

0.2.0-monocles2 2026-10-22 am
Wire format unchanged.
Mesh maintenance: a call whose last other participant left ends, whichever of the leg's session-terminate and the participant's presence arrives first; a call nobody has connected to yet keeps waiting.
Leaving: hang-up from any place ends the whole conference; leaving a call others continue suppresses that call's invite until it is over.
New section on concurrent calls (busy rules) and call history.
0.2.0-monocles1 2026-10-18 am
monocles chat profile; wire format unchanged from 0.2.0.
Add the optional 'device' attribute on <muji/> (OMEMO device id of the participant).
Participant authentication: non-anonymous rooms only, real full JIDs only, incoming session-initiates bound to the MUC-vouched real JID of a READY participant.
Deterministic occupant-JID tie-break instead of "the joiner initiates".
DTLS fingerprint protection per leg (opportunistic and PQ OMEMO2-verified modes; no legacy-OMEMO downgrade and trusted identities only in verified mode).
Presence persistence: every self-presence sent to the room carries <muji/>; leaving/being removed from the room ends the call; nick changes keep legs.
Mesh maintenance (stuck-leg retirement, periodic re-mesh, leg identity on teardown, crossed-initiate resolution).
Conference-wide audio→video upgrade (content-add / senders content-modify per leg, automatic receive-only acceptance, retry back-off).
Privacy and resource limits: no group calls over Tor/I2P, blocked JIDs excluded, participant cap, invites suppressed in muted rooms.

section1.p: &xep0166; is used to negotiate peer to peer media sessions. Muji (short for Multiparty Jingle) is a way to coordinate Jingle sessions between a group of people. Muji conferences are held in &xep0045; rooms.

Version 0.2.0 of this specification describes the coordination protocol but leaves open how participants are authenticated, how the per-pair media sessions are protected against an active attacker, and how a long-running full-mesh call survives presence updates, nick changes, reconnects and flaky legs. This document is the monocles profile of XEP-0272: it does not change any element defined by 0.2.0 (implementations of 0.2.0 interoperate with it), and it adds the rules that monocles chat implements. Sections and requirements introduced by the profile are marked "(monocles)".
The keywords "MUST", "SHOULD", "MAY" etc. are to be interpreted as described in &rfc2119;.

A Muji conference has a number of contents, each of which has unique name, content type, and an encoding. Each participant may provide a stream for each content, and communicates which contents they are willing to provide streams for, along with encoding information, in their MUC presence. This serves two purposes. Firstly, so that each participant knows which contents every other participant provides. Secondly, so that there is a global payload type (PT) mapping for the various contents, so that clients only need to encode and payload each content that they provide once.
Participants are not required to participate all the contents that are available. For example, a Muji client might choose to only request audio streams.

(monocles) Conferences are run as a full mesh: every pair of participants holds exactly one ordinary &xep0167; session (a leg), with ICE (&xep0176;) and DTLS-SRTP (&xep0320;). There is no server-side mixer, so media is end-to-end encrypted between each pair of participants and its integrity depends on the authenticity of the DTLS fingerprint exchanged on that leg (see DTLS Fingerprint Protection).
(monocles)

Jingle sessions are addressed to the participants' real JIDs, and every leg is authenticated against the real JID of the participant (see Participant Authentication). A client therefore MUST NOT start or join a Muji conference in a room that does not reveal real JIDs to it. monocles chat only offers group calls in rooms that are both members-only and non-anonymous ("private group chats"), and refuses to place one otherwise.

Advertisements from occupants whose real JID is not provided by the room, or is not a full JID, MUST be ignored: the client neither initiates a leg to nor accepts a leg from such an occupant. A client MUST NOT fall back to addressing the occupant JID.

Joining a conference is done in two stages. The first step is to declare that preparations are being done to either join or start a Muji session inside the MUC. This is indicated by the client sending a presence stanza to the MUC with a preparing element in the Muji section.
section1.code: <presence from='wiccarocks@shakespeare.lit/laptop' to='darkcave@chat.shakespeare.lit/oldhag'> <c xmlns="http://jabber.org/protocol/caps" node="https://monocles.eu" ver="48QdBuXRCJFb8qIzgy1FOHSGO0U=" hash="sha-1" /> <muji xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:muji:0' device='1823562411'> <preparing /> </muji> </presence>
section1.p: The client MUST then wait until the MUC rebroadcasts its presence message, after which it MUST wait for all other participants that had a preparing element in their presence to finish preparation. Afterwards it should finish its own preparation by updating its presence with the contents it wants to take part in.
section1.code: <presence from='wiccarocks@shakespeare.lit/laptop' to='darkcave@chat.shakespeare.lit/oldhag'> <muji xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:muji:0' device='1823562411'> <content creator='initiator' name='voice'> <description xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:apps:rtp:1' media='audio'> <payload-type id='111' name='opus' clockrate='48000' channels='2'/> </description> </content> <content creator='initiator' name='webcam'> <description xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:apps:rtp:1' media='video'> <payload-type id='96' name='VP8' clockrate='90000'/> </description> </content> </muji> </presence>
section1.p: When a client adds a payload ID to a content description, it MUST have the same codec name and receiving parameters as the corresponding entries in other participants' payload maps for that content. For instance, if Alice defines a payload type with ID 98, codec Speex and a clock rate of 8000 for a content called “voice0”, then Bob must define payload type 98 identically or not at all for that content.

Furthermore, each content description MUST include at least one payload type that every other participant supports. In other words, the intersection of payload type mappings in descriptions for a content must not be the empty set. This avoids clients having to encode the same stream multiple times, which can be very costly, and also allows sending the encoded data only once where the transport makes this possible (e.g. IP multicast).

(monocles) A participant is READY when its <muji/> element contains at least one <content/> and no <preparing/>; a <muji/> with <preparing/>, or with neither child, is PREPARING. Only READY participants are meshed with. monocles chat uses a fixed codec set (Opus for 'voice', VP8 for 'webcam'), so it advertises <preparing/> and its ready contents back-to-back; the advertised payload types are advisory and every leg still runs a complete SDP offer/answer.

section2.p: The <muji/> element MAY carry a 'device' attribute holding the participant's OMEMO device id (a decimal integer in the range 1..231-1). It tells the other participants which of the participant's devices is in the call, so that the DTLS fingerprint of a leg can be encrypted to exactly that device. A value outside the range, or one that does not parse, MUST be treated as absent. Clients that do not implement this profile ignore the attribute.

Once a client has constructed content descriptions and advertised them in its MUC presence, it MUST initiate a Jingle session with every other participant. The requirement that it is the joining participant that initiates sessions avoids race conditions.

Jingle sessions are initiated between the real JIDs of participants, since IQ routing is not guaranteed to work in &xep0045; and in &xep0369;. To indicate that a Jingle session-initiate belongs to a MUJI conference, a <muji> element is placed in the <jingle> element. The receiver SHOULD only assume that a Jingle session-initiate belongs to a Muji conference if the sender is actually part of the referenced MUC. Content names inside Muji-related Jingle sessions always refer to the content with the same name inside the Muji conference.

example.caption: Jingle session-initiate referencing a Muji conference

section2.example: <iq to='wiccarocks@shakespeare.lit/laptop' type='set' id='id1'> <jingle xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:1' action='session-initiate' initiator='hag66@shakespeare.lit/mobile' sid='sid1'> <muji room='darkcave@chat.shakespeare.lit' xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:muji:0' /> <content creator='initiator' name='this-is-a-stub'> <description xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:apps:stub:0'/> <transport xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:transports:stub:0'/> </content> </jingle> </iq>
section2.p: (monocles) Muji legs are not announced with &xep0353; (no ringing): the user has already joined the call, so a valid incoming Muji session-initiate is accepted automatically. This is exactly why the authentication rules below are mandatory.

(monocles) Both clients follow the rule to wait until the MUC has rebroadcast their own presence. They start their legs only after the room has reflected their READY <muji/>. A session-initiate is sent directly, while the presence travels through the room, so an earlier initiate can reach a peer before the peer knows the sender is a participant. The peer then refuses it, and the leg only comes up on a later retry. If no reflection arrives within 5 seconds, the client starts its legs anyway. Incoming legs are accepted in the meantime.

"The joiner initiates" is not enough for a long-running mesh: a leg can fail mid-call and must be re-established by someone, and two participants joining at the same time are both "the joiner". monocles chat therefore decides the initiator of every leg deterministically: of the two participants' nicks (the resource parts of their occupant JIDs), the one that is greater in lexicographic (UTF-16 code unit) order initiates, and the other waits for the session-initiate. Only the nicks are compared. The room is the same for both by definition, but clients may spell it differently (bare JIDs are case-insensitive). Comparing the whole occupant JID let two clients disagree, so that each waited for the other. Clients that follow the 0.2.0 rule interoperate: their initiates are accepted regardless of the tie-break (see Crossed Initiates).
The tie-break uses the client's current occupant JID. After a nick change the client MUST use its new occupant JID.

section1.p: (monocles)

A Muji leg is auto-accepted, so the receiver MUST verify that the sender really is a participant before accepting it. A client MUST terminate an incoming session-initiate carrying <muji room='R'/> unless all of the following hold:

ol.li: The client is itself currently in the conference held in room R. R is compared as a bare JID, case-insensitively: peers may spell the room differently from the client's own copy. A raw string comparison declines every leg such a peer starts, and the call then reconnects in a loop.

The session-initiate's 'from' equals the real full JID that room R reported (in the <item jid=''/> of &xep0045;) for an occupant whose latest presence in R advertises <muji/> (preparing or ready). The initiate is sent directly to us, while the READY presence travels through the MUC, so the initiate can arrive first. The 'room' attribute itself is attacker-controlled and only selects which room's participant list is consulted. If no participant matches the full JID, the client MAY accept the leg when exactly one participant has the sender's bare JID. This happens when the room still reports an older session of that account, for example after a client restart or with a multi-session nick. That participant is then addressed at the calling full JID. The account is still the one the MUC vouched for, and on a verified call the fingerprint must still come from the advertised OMEMO device.
The sender is not on the client's block list (neither its bare JID nor its domain).
Accepting it does not exceed the participant limit (see Limits).
The client is allowed to run peer-to-peer media on the current connection (see Privacy Considerations).

section1.p: The same filters apply in the other direction: a client MUST NOT initiate a leg to an occupant that fails rules 2–5.

The real JID is vouched for by the MUC service. The participant list is rebuilt whenever the client (re)joins the room — all participant state from before the (re)join MUST be discarded, because the room replays the presence of every current occupant on join and occupants that left in the meantime would otherwise linger.
(monocles)

DTLS-SRTP only protects a leg if the fingerprint each side receives is the fingerprint the other side sent. In 0.2.0 it travels in cleartext through both parties' servers, which can substitute it and run a man-in-the-middle on the media. monocles chat therefore encrypts the <fingerprint/> of every leg with OMEMO, using the same element that monocles and Conversations use for 1:1 calls: the &xep0320; fingerprint is replaced by a <fingerprint xmlns='http://gultsch.de/xmpp/drafts/omemo/dlts-srtp-verification'/> that keeps the cleartext 'setup' and 'hash' attributes and carries an OMEMO-encrypted payload holding the real fingerprint.

example.caption: Encrypted DTLS fingerprint inside a Muji leg's transport (PQ OMEMO2)

section1.example: <transport xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:transports:ice-udp:1' ufrag='8hhy' pwd='asd88fgpdd777uzjYhagZg'> <fingerprint xmlns='http://gultsch.de/xmpp/drafts/omemo/dlts-srtp-verification' setup='actpass' hash='sha-256'> <encrypted xmlns='urn:monocles:omemo-pq:1'> <!-- OMEMO2 (PQXDH) header + SCE payload; the SCE <content> holds <fingerprint xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:apps:dtls:0' setup='actpass' hash='sha-256'> 02:1A:CC:…:5F </fingerprint> --> </encrypted> </fingerprint> </transport>
section1.p: The fingerprint is encrypted to the peer's real bare JID and the device id taken from the peer's <muji device=''/>. The sender's OMEMO session is looked up for the real JID of the leg, never for the occupant JID. On receipt, the device id that decrypted the payload MUST equal the advertised device id. A mismatch MUST terminate the leg, and this check MUST happen before the fingerprint is recorded. Every later encrypted fingerprint on the same leg (session-accept, content-add, transport-replace) MUST carry the same fingerprint from the same device.

section2.p: The protection level of a call is chosen by the participant who places or joins it, from the encryption selected for the group chat at that moment:

ul.li: Opportunistic (group chat unencrypted, or legacy OMEMO selected): the client encrypts the fingerprint when it can (any OMEMO stack, any trust state) and otherwise falls back to a cleartext fingerprint. A cleartext fingerprint from the peer is accepted. The call is protected against passive observers but not against an active attacker on the signalling path.

Verified (post-quantum OMEMO2, urn:monocles:omemo-pq:1, selected): on every leg the client
MUST NOT send a cleartext fingerprint. If it cannot encrypt, the leg fails instead of being downgraded.
MUST encrypt with OMEMO2 only. It MUST NOT build, use or accept a legacy (eu.siacs.conversations.axolotl) session for the fingerprint, and MUST reject a legacy-wrapped fingerprint before handing it to any ratchet (strict stack separation).
MUST encrypt to, and accept from, only an identity that the user trusts and that is active. These are the same keys an OMEMO2 message to that contact would be encrypted to. An untrusted or undecided identity fails the leg.
MUST reject a cleartext fingerprint from the peer.

section2.p: The mode is enforced per participant and per leg. If Alice placed the call in verified mode and Bob runs it opportunistically, the Alice–Bob leg only comes up if Bob's client can and does send an OMEMO2-encrypted fingerprint. Otherwise only that leg is refused, not the whole call. Nothing about the mode is signalled on the wire, so an attacker cannot negotiate it down.

section1.p: (monocles)

A presence of a participant without <muji/> means that the participant left the call (Leaving a Conference). Clients refresh their MUC presence for many unrelated reasons, such as a status or avatar change, the room gaining &xep0421; support, a nick change, or a reconnect that requires a re-join. While a client is in a conference, it MUST include its current READY <muji/> element in every presence it sends to that room, including the join presence of a re-join. If the room reflects a self-presence of the client without <muji/> while the client is still in the call, the client SHOULD re-announce its <muji/> immediately.
Directed presence updates for the call MUST be sent to the client's current occupant JID. A presence to a stale nick is a rename request in &xep0045; and would silently undo a nick change.

Nick changes (an unavailable presence with status code 303 followed by the presence under the new nick) MUST NOT tear down the renamed participant's leg: legs are keyed by real JID, and the participant has not left. If the real JID behind an occupant JID changes, the leg to the previous real JID MUST be ended.

If the client receives its own unavailable presence from the room without status code 303 (it left, was kicked or banned, or the room was destroyed), or leaves the room itself, it MUST end every leg of that room's conference and forget the room's participant list. It MUST NOT send any further presence to the room for the call, because a directed presence to the room would re-join it.
(monocles)
A full mesh only keeps working if broken legs are repaired. monocles chat reconciles the mesh periodically (every 8 seconds) while it is in a call:

ol.li: A leg that ended, failed ICE, or has not reached the connected state within 12 seconds of being (re)started is terminated and forgotten.
For every READY participant without a leg, the tie-break is applied again, and the client initiates the leg if it is the initiator.

section1.p: A participant leaving does not end the call for the others. A client stays in the conference as long as it has a live leg or at least one other participant advertises <muji/> (in any state). It leaves on its own only when both are gone and at least one of its legs had connected during the call; a call that nobody has joined yet keeps waiting. When it leaves, it retracts its <muji/> first.

A participant that hangs up sends its presence without <muji/> through the room and its session-terminate directly, so the two can arrive in either order. A client MUST therefore check whether it is left alone both when a leg ends and when a participant's <muji/> goes away. Checking only when a leg ends leaves a client alone in an empty call if the leg ended while the participant still appeared to be present.

section2.p: Legs are identified by the peer's real full JID, and at most one leg per peer is live. When a leg is replaced, the replaced leg's teardown MUST NOT remove the bookkeeping of the leg that replaced it. Implementations SHOULD compare the leg object or session id, not only the peer JID.

A participant can receive a session-initiate from a peer it already has a leg with. This happens when the peer restarted a stuck leg, or when both sides started a leg at once. The second case occurs when the two sides disagree on the tie-break, for example because the server rewrote a nick or a JID differs in case, or with a 0.2.0 client that always initiates on join. The receiver keeps its existing leg and terminates the new initiate if the existing leg is connected. Otherwise it keeps the leg whose Jingle session id ('sid') is smaller in lexicographic order, and terminates the other one. Both sides compare the same two session ids, so they always keep the same leg. A rule based on the occupant-JID tie-break could make each side terminate the other's leg on every retry, and the call would never connect.

section1.p: To leave a conference the Muji information MUST first be removed from the participant's presence; subsequently it SHOULD terminate all Jingle sessions related to that conference. Updating the presence first reduces the likelihood of situations where new participants initiate sessions with participants who are leaving the conference.

(monocles) The call UI is per call, not per leg: hanging up ends the whole conference, wherever the user hangs up (the call window or an ongoing-call notification). Ending a single leg, because its participant left or because the client retired a stuck leg (Mesh Maintenance), never ends the conference. A client that leaves the call but stays in the room keeps the room's participant list, so that re-joining the call meshes with the participants who are still in it, even though they do not resend their presence.

(monocles) After leaving a call that the others continue, the client treats the call's invite as already shown (Limits). Otherwise the next presence of any remaining participant, such as a status or avatar change, would offer the user the call they just left.
Adding a stream follows a process similar to the joining of a conference. As a first step, an updated presence stanza MUST be sent which contains a preparing element as part of the Muji section.
section1.code: <presence from='wiccarocks@shakespeare.lit/laptop' to='darkcave@chat.shakespeare.lit/oldhag'> <muji xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:muji:0'> <content creator='initiator' name='voice'> <description xmlns='urn:xmpp:jingle:apps:rtp:1' media='audio'> <payload-type id='111' name='opus' clockrate='48000' channels='2'/> </description> </content> <preparing/> </muji> </presence>
section1.p: The client MUST then wait until the MUC rebroadcasts its presence message, after which it MUST wait for all other participants that had a preparing element in their presence to finish their changes.
Afterwards the client should add the new content to the Muji section of its presence and add the content to all the Jingle sessions it had with participants it shared the content with.

(monocles) A participant that joins an audio+video conference audio-only sends only audio. It answers the video content of an offer with 'senders' restricted to the peer, so it still sees the other participants' video without turning on its camera.

(monocles) Turning the camera on during a call (upgrading from audio to video) is done for the whole conference, never only for one leg. The participant re-announces its presence (<preparing/>, then the contents including 'webcam'), sets up new legs with video from then on, and brings its camera onto every existing leg as follows:

ul.li: If the leg has no video content yet, the participant sends a content-add with senders='both'.

If the leg already has a video content on which the participant only receives, it sends a content-modify that changes 'senders' to 'both'. The peer applies it and acknowledges the IQ. Neither side sends an SDP answer for this change: each side completes its WebRTC offer/answer locally from the agreed 'senders'.

section1.p: (monocles) A participant receiving a video content-add on a Muji leg accepts it without asking the user, because the user has already joined the call. If it is not sending video itself, it first narrows the content's 'senders' to the adding party with a content-modify on the pending content-add (&xep0166;) and then sends a receive-only content-accept. If it is sending video, it accepts the content with 'senders' left at 'both'.

(monocles) Crossed content-adds on the same leg are resolved like in &xep0166;: the session initiator answers the responder's content-add with a <tie-break/> error, and the responder accepts the initiator's. If the peer rejects or refuses a camera, the client keeps receiving, stops offering to send on that leg, and tries again after a back-off of 30 seconds instead of in a loop. The periodic re-mesh also re-checks that every connected leg carries the participant's camera. This covers a participant who joined audio-only and initiated the leg to a video participant: the video participant adds its camera to that leg once the leg is connected.

To remove a content type, the participant SHOULD first send an updated presence without the content in its Muji section. Afterwards, it MUST remove the content from all the Jingle sessions it has open.
(monocles)

In a full mesh every participant runs one ICE agent and one PeerConnection, and uploads one copy of its media, per other participant. Any occupant can start advertising <muji/>, so without a bound a large or hostile room could exhaust a device's CPU, memory or uplink. A client MUST bound the number of legs it maintains. monocles chat meshes with at most 8 other participants (a 9-person call), and refuses or skips further legs. Calls of that size and larger need a relay or mixer (Relays and Mixers).

Because any occupant can toggle <muji/>, the "join the group call" notification is shown at most once per room until the call is over, and it is not shown for rooms the user has muted. Leaving a call counts as having shown its notification: it is offered again only for a new call, after every participant of the previous one has gone.

When scaling to conferences with a big number of participants it's no longer viable for all participants to have direct connections.
On connections where upstream bandwidth is the limiting factor, an RTP relay which is able to relay the stream to multiple participants on the behalf of the clients and which forwards the streams of other participants back to the client can be used.
If the limiting factor is either CPU or downstream bandwidth then a mixer can be used, which receives the media streams from other participants and mixes them on behalf of the client, so that the client only has to deal with receiving and decoding a single stream for each media type. On the sending side a mixer acts like a relay and relays the clients stream to all other participants.
Both these services can either be provided by dedicated services or by other clients.

(monocles) A relay or mixer terminates DTLS-SRTP and therefore sees the media in cleartext, which defeats the end-to-end protection described above. monocles chat does not use relays or mixers. TURN servers are only used as ICE relays, and they carry SRTP that they cannot decrypt.
To invite someone to a Muji conference, a &xep0482; <invite> is sent containing a <muji> element in the urn:xmpp:jingle:muji:0 namespace with a 'room' attribute specifying the JID of the Muji MUC.

(monocles) monocles chat for Android does not send &xep0482; invites yet. An occupant of the room learns about a running call from the participants' <muji/> presence, and is offered a "join" notification for it.
(monocles)
A client runs at most one call at a time, and a conference counts as a call from the moment the client joins it, including while it waits alone with no leg yet. While it is in a conference:

ul.li: An incoming 1:1 call (a &xep0353; <propose/>) does not ring. The client records it as a missed call. It MAY reject it as busy, but only if no other device of the user's account could answer it; otherwise it leaves the call to the other devices.
The client does not start a 1:1 call or join a second conference.

section1.p: During a 1:1 call, the client does not start or join a conference. Session-initiates of the conference's own legs (tagged with <muji room/>) are never refused as busy; they are part of the call the client is already in.

A client keeps one call-history entry per conference it took part in, not one per leg. The entry is incoming if the client joined a call that was already running and at least one leg connected, and outgoing otherwise. A conference in which no leg connected is never shown as a missed call: legs are retried and retired all the time (Mesh Maintenance), and one entry per leg would flood the history with missed calls.

ul.li: Unsolicited media. Muji legs are accepted without ringing. Without the checks in Participant Authentication, any entity that learns a user is in a call could inject a media session by sending a session-initiate with a forged 'room' attribute.

Trust in the MUC service. The binding between occupant and real JID comes from the room. A malicious MUC service can claim any real JID for an occupant. In opportunistic mode it can therefore insert itself into a call. In verified mode it cannot, because the fingerprint has to be encrypted with an OMEMO2 identity that the user trusts for that real JID.

Signalling-path man-in-the-middle. Cleartext DTLS fingerprints can be swapped by either party's server. Verified mode closes this per leg. Opportunistic mode does not, and clients SHOULD make the difference visible to the user.

Downgrade. In verified mode, a failed OMEMO2 encryption, a legacy-only peer, an untrusted identity or a cleartext fingerprint each fail the leg. Nothing falls back silently. The mode is not signalled on the wire, so it cannot be negotiated away.
Device binding. The decrypting device id is checked against the device advertised in <muji device=''/>. Another device of the same account cannot take over the leg.

Resource exhaustion. There is a participant cap, see Limits. Because a camera content-add is accepted without asking, a client MUST also limit the number of video contents per leg. monocles uses a limit of 2: the peer's camera, plus a second m-line when one side upgrades over a receive-only one. It refuses further content-adds with content-reject.

Renegotiation keeps verification. If a leg's DTLS fingerprint was OMEMO-authenticated at setup, every later fingerprint on that leg (content-add, content-accept) MUST also be encrypted and come from the same OMEMO identity and device. Otherwise the leg is terminated with security-error. Without this rule a renegotiation could quietly drop the verification of a running call. This applies in opportunistic mode as well.

Camera privacy. When a client adds its camera to a leg, or accepts a peer's camera with its own, it MUST keep the user's camera-off choice for the conference. A leg that newly carries video sends black frames while the camera is off, never the live camera.

Spoofed participants. Only presences from occupants of a group chat the client has joined may change Muji state. A contact's ordinary presence (user@host/resource) carrying a forged <muji/> and muc#user item MUST be ignored. Otherwise it could add fake participants and trigger "join group call" prompts.
Robustness. Muji presence and Jingle payloads come from other occupants. Malformed values (such as a non-numeric or out-of-range 'device') MUST be ignored and MUST NOT abort stanza processing.

ICE reveals the participant's IP addresses to every other participant (host and server-reflexive candidates) and to the TURN server. A client that connects through Tor or I2P, or whose account is an onion or I2P account, MUST NOT place, join or accept a Muji call. This is the same rule that monocles chat applies to 1:1 calls, and it is enforced both in the UI and when an incoming leg is accepted.
Muji needs real JIDs, so every participant learns the real JID of every other participant. This is why Muji is limited to non-anonymous rooms, where real JIDs are visible anyway.
The 'device' attribute reveals the OMEMO device id of the device in the call to all occupants of the room. The device id is already public in the account's PEP device list.
Blocked users are excluded from the mesh in both directions.

section1.p: This profile changes no element, so a 0.2.0 implementation can join a call with monocles clients. In that case:

ul.li: Its cleartext fingerprint is accepted only by participants that run the call opportunistically.
Its initiates are always considered, whatever the tie-break says (see Crossed Initiates).
Its legs may be torn down if it sends room presence without <muji/> while in the call.

section1.p: monocles chat for Android and monocles chat desktop implement the same wire format and the same rules: the 'device' attribute, the <muji room/> marker, the tie-break, the encrypted fingerprint, the verified mode, presence persistence and the call-wide audio→video upgrade. Two differences remain. The desktop client has no Tor/I2P transport and no block list (XEP-0191), so those two rules do not apply to it. It also never changes 'senders' on an m-line it receives on: to start sending, it always adds a new video content with content-add, which the other clients accept like any other camera.

Every client MUST put honest 'senders' values on the contents of a Muji leg. If a client advertises 'both' for an m-line it only receives on, its peers wait for video that never comes (and show an empty tile). It also breaks the summary check that matches a content-accept to its content-add.
This document requires no interaction with the IANA.
No new namespaces. The profile reuses urn:xmpp:jingle:muji:0 and adds the optional 'device' attribute to its <muji/> element.
